title: Fitting a shower bath screen with a pivot panel
subtitle: Fix a hinged glass screen to the end of a bath for an open shower area
excerpt: How to fit a pivot-panel shower bath screen to the tap end of a bathtub. Covers drilling into the bath surround, fitting the wall channel, hanging the screen, and sealing the base rail.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK plumbing trade practice for bathroom fitting.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hinged single-panel or double-panel glass screen fitted at the tap end of a bath to contain shower spray. The pivot hinge allows the screen to swing open for bath access. The screen attaches to a wall channel on one side and rests on a base seal or bottom rail on the bath rim.

The vertical aluminium extrusion that is fixed to the wall and carries one edge of the bath screen. The screen glass or frame clicks or slides into the channel. The channel is drilled into the wall with the screen manufacturer's supplied fixings.

content.text: A
pivot bath screen
fits at the shower end of a bath and stops water reaching the bathroom floor when you shower standing up. The screen fixes to a
wall channel
on one side and rests on a base rail sitting on the bath rim. The work is drilling, levelling, and siliconing.
Before you start: check the wall and bath rim

Most bath screens need a clear vertical run of solid wall 50 to 70 mm wide for the wall channel. If the bath sits against a tiled wall, the tiles are the substrate; drill through them with a tile drill bit at slow speed with no hammer action until you reach the substrate, then switch to a masonry bit. Check whether the bath rim is level along its length with a spirit level. A rim that drops away from the wall means the base rail will not seal without packing. The screen manufacturer's instructions will state whether the screen can be adjusted for a rim that is out of level.
Step 1: Mark the wall channel position

Hold the wall channel against the wall at the correct end of the bath with the inner face of the channel sitting flush with the bath rim edge. Use a spirit level to check the channel is plumb. Mark the fixing holes in pencil through the channel onto the wall. Most channels have two or three fixings. Double-check the plumb before drilling.
Step 2: Drill and plug the wall

Apply masking tape to tiled walls over the drill marks to stop the bit skating. Drill to the depth of the supplied wall plugs. For tiles over masonry, drill through the tile at low speed (no hammer) with a tile bit, then change to a masonry bit and drill into the wall at hammer speed. Blow the dust out and push in the wall plugs. The channel fixings in a typical screen kit are M4 or M5 machine screws; do not overtighten into plastic plugs.
Step 3: Fix the wall channel

Apply a bead of neutral-cure silicone sealant down the back face of the wall channel before fixing (some manufacturers supply a gasket instead). Press the channel onto the wall, align the fixing screws, and tighten. Wipe away any silicone that squeezes out with a damp cloth. Check the channel is still plumb after tightening.
Step 4: Hang the screen

Screen assembly varies between manufacturers, but the typical method is to slide the screen hinge post into the wall channel from the top, then lower until the hinge pin engages. On models where the glass is separate from the frame, the glass slides into the frame last, secured by a plastic retaining strip. Follow the specific assembly sequence in the instructions. Do not force any component.
Step 5: Fit the base rail and seal

Lower the base rail (or bottom wiper seal) onto the bath rim. On most screens the base rail is adjustable for minor height variation. Check the rail is flush with the inner face of the bath rim. Run a bead of clear silicone along the outer face of the base rail where it meets the bath rim and along the wall-channel-to-wall joint. Smooth the silicone bead with a wet finger. Leave the sealant to cure for 24 hours before using the shower.
Variations
Fold-over screens have two panels, one fixed and one that folds inward over the bath for access. The fixing method is the same; the second panel adds a pivot hinge in the middle of the screen.
Free-standing bath screens fix to a floor-mounted post rather than a wall channel. The post is bolted to the floor through the bath panel; the seal is between the screen edge and the bath rim only.
If the bath is in a recess with walls on three sides, fit a fixed straight panel on the far side and a pivot panel on the entry side.
Care

Wipe the screen dry after each shower to slow limescale build-up on the glass. Clean the bottom rail seal monthly with a mildew remover and check the silicone at the wall channel annually. Replace the silicone bead when it shows black mould that will not clean off, or when it starts to separate from the wall or bath rim.

attrs.symptom: Water escapes under the base rail
attrs.cause: The base seal is not sitting flush on the bath rim, or the silicone bead has a gap.
attrs.fix: Lift the base rail, clean off old silicone, and re-bed with a continuous bead of silicone. Allow to cure fully before using the shower.

attrs.symptom: Screen swings open when the shower is running
attrs.cause: The pivot hinge has no built-in tension, or the tension adjuster has loosened.
attrs.fix: Check the manufacturer's instructions for the tension adjuster screw on the pivot hinge. Tighten until the screen stays open only when pushed deliberately.

attrs.symptom: Wall channel not plumb after fixing
attrs.cause: The wall surface was not flat, or the channel was tightened unevenly.
attrs.fix: Remove the channel, re-mark the fixing holes with a fresh plumb check, and re-fix. Shim behind the channel with thin plastic packers if the wall surface is uneven.
